author: prabal04das
content: So, it is like while going offline, it saves the sync committee and after coming online, it starts from that committee up to current sync committee linearly. If so, then how long can the client remain offline before its stored sync committee is considered unsafe? Thanks for the clarifications 🙂

author: dirkjaeckel
content: Why would a past verified sync committee be considered unsafe ever? The only problem I see is that the sync committee is so old that the client has a harder time finding cl nodes that still serve the update. In my experience a month's old sync committee update is not a problem.

author: prabal04das
content: That's fair in practice, but even if acquiring old keys has a high coordination barrier in practice, how does the client formally defend against long-range attacks once the weak subjectivity period passes? In that scenario, does Myotis invalidate its stored state and require the user to bootstrap again from a fresh trusted checkpoint?

author: dirkjaeckel
content: Thank you for pointing this out! ATM the weak subjectivity period is ignored. I will change this to the following behaviour: 1. If the trust anchor (block root) is older than the chains weak subjectivity period and the last LC update is also not newer there will be a warning to the user with an explanation and the user will be able to enter their own block root for a more recent period. 2. ATM the android app updates the LC every night if power is connected. If the last LC update is older than the WS period there is again a warning to the user with the ability to ignore it. 3. Every proper release will contain an updated block root as the trust anchor

author: dirkjaeckel
content: Unfortunately the WS period for mainnet seems to be only 2 weeks. I am not sure I will make a release every 2 weeks. But maybe I should.

author: dirkjaeckel
content: As long as the app is started every week and loads the latest LC updates an update of the embedded checkpoint (block root) should not be necessary.
